## How to choose a CRM

- Want to start at $0? Zoho CRM’s free edition covers up to 3 users; Attio’s free plan covers up to 3 seats and 50,000 records; HubSpot’s free CRM covers up to 2 users and 1,000 contacts.
- A team of three or more? monday CRM sells seats from a minimum of 3. Basic is $12 per seat a month billed yearly ($18 monthly), with a 14-day trial and no card.
- Need email sync and automations? They are not on every entry plan. Pipedrive adds two-way email sync and automations at Growth ($39 per seat on annual billing), not Lite. noCRM.io offers two-way email sync on Dream ($39).
- Lead-driven sales team? noCRM.io is built around leads rather than contacts and offers a 15-day trial with no card.
- Planning to grow into a big platform? Salesforce Starter Suite is $25 per user a month, billed monthly or annually, with a 30-day free trial.
- Budget for year two. HubSpot’s Starter price of $7 a seat is a limited-time offer for new customers; HubSpot says the normal price is $20.

## Common questions

Which CRM here has the biggest free plan?

By user count, Zoho CRM and Attio: Zoho’s free edition allows up to 3 users, and Attio’s free plan allows up to 3 seats and 50,000 records. HubSpot’s free CRM allows up to 2 users and 1,000 contacts. Pipedrive, noCRM.io, Salesforce and monday CRM have free trials instead of free plans.

Which CRMs let me try without a credit card?

Pipedrive (14 days), noCRM.io (15 days), monday CRM (14 days) and Salesforce Starter Suite (30 days) all say their trials need no credit card. noCRM.io lets you extend to 30 days by adding payment details.

Do HubSpot’s Professional and Enterprise plans have setup fees?

Yes. HubSpot’s product catalogue lists a one-time required onboarding fee of $1,500 for Sales Hub Professional and $3,500 for Enterprise.

How much do I save paying annually?

It varies. Pipedrive says up to 42%, noCRM.io up to 40%. Zoho CRM’s annual prices are lower than monthly (Standard $14 vs $20). monday CRM shows “Save 33%” on yearly billing and Attio says 20%. Salesforce Starter costs the same either way.

Best CRM Software for Small Teams (2026): Price It by the Seat, Not the Feature List | Small Business Software Guide

# Best CRM Software for Small Teams (2026): Price It by the Seat, Not the Feature List

By Russell Vale

Last updated 2026-11-10

The short answer: price it by the seat, not the feature list. Freshsales Growth ($9/user/month billed annually) is the cheapest paid pick with real sales tools — pipeline, email, phone, and chat in one place. Zoho CRM Standard ($14/user/month billed annually) is the pick for the most room to grow, with a free tier for up to 3 users. Pipedrive Lite ($14/seat/month billed annually) is the pick for a team that lives in its pipeline and wants nothing else. monday CRM Basic ($12/seat/month billed annually) is the pick for visual, operations-heavy teams. Bigin Express ($7/user/month billed annually) is the pick for micro-teams of one or two. HubSpot free ($0) is where a two-person team should start — and Less Annoying CRM ($15/user/month, one flat price) is the pick if you want the simplest possible decision. The number that decides between them is your headcount, not the brochure.

> Affiliate disclosure. We don’t have affiliate partnerships with any vendor yet, so every link below is a plain link to the vendor’s own site — nobody pays us for clicks or signups, and that won’t change what we recommend. If we add affiliate programs later, this article will say so.

## The small-team equation: per-seat pricing makes headcount the price

A small team’s CRM problem is different from a startup’s and different from an enterprise’s, and the difference is arithmetic. Define the team first: 2 to 10 people sharing one pipeline, no dedicated administrator, and the person choosing the software is usually also the person selling. Three things shape the decision.

First, per-seat pricing means the bill scales linearly with headcount. Nearly every CRM here charges per user per month, so a 5-person team pays five times the headline price. The gap between the cheapest and the most expensive pick in this guide is $7 versus $25 per seat — at 5 seats that is $35 versus $125 a month, or $420 versus $1,500 a year, for tools that all do the same core job: remember who you talked to, what was promised, and when to follow up. Run the math at your real headcount before comparing features, because a feature list never mentions that the bill triples when you hire two more people.

Second, the free tier ends at a seat count, not a date. HubSpot free covers 2 users, Zoho and Freshsales free cover 3, Bigin free covers 1, Capsule free covers 2. None of these expire — they end the day your next hire needs a login. That makes the free tier a runway, not a home: a two-person team on HubSpot free has until its third hire, a three-person team on Zoho free has until its fourth. Plan the paid step now, while the switch is still cheap, instead of discovering it mid-quarter when the new hire cannot see the pipeline.

Third, adoption is the whole game, and complexity kills it. A CRM that takes weeks to configure is a CRM that won’t get used — and at this size there is no admin to force it. The honest test is whether the least technical person on the team will open it every morning without being told. That is why the simplest tools on this list (Bigin, Less Annoying CRM, Pipedrive) keep winning small-team recommendations against more powerful ones: a pipeline everyone updates beats a platform nobody opens.

So pick by the math and the team, not the marketing:

- Cheapest real sales tool — you want Freshsales Growth ($9/user/month).
- Most room to grow — you want Zoho CRM Standard ($14/user/month).
- Pipeline-first selling — you want Pipedrive Lite ($14/seat/month).
- Visual workflows and operations — you want monday CRM Basic ($12/seat/month).
- Micro-team of one or two — you want Bigin Express ($7/user/month).
- Two people, zero budget — you want HubSpot free.
- Simplest possible decision — you want Less Annoying CRM ($15/user/month flat).

## The free tiers, and when free stops being enough

Start free — four options here run indefinitely at $0, and the follow-up habit matters more than the tool. But every free tier ends, and each one ends at a different wall.

| Free plan | Caps | First paid step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HubSpot | 2 users, 1,000 marketing contacts, no donor-style extras needed here | Sales Starter: $20/seat/month (list price; currently shown at a $7 promotional rate for new customers on annual billing) |
| Zoho CRM | Up to 3 users, leads, contacts, deals, mobile apps | Standard: $14/user/month billed annually |
| Freshsales | Up to 3 users, contact and deal management, built-in chat | Growth: $9/user/month billed annually |
| Bigin | 1 user, pipeline and contacts | Express: $7/user/month billed annually |
| Capsule | 2 users, 250 contacts, one pipeline, 5 custom fields | Professional: $18/user/month billed annually |

When free stops being enough: the seat cap ends the free run first. HubSpot’s 2-user limit forces a paid seat at your third hire; Zoho’s and Freshsales’ 3-user limits force one at your fourth. The feature ceiling ends it second, and the ceiling is different on each tool: HubSpot free has no real sales automation — that waits at Sales Hub Professional, $90/seat/month plus a mandatory $1,500 onboarding fee. Zoho free has workflow automation included, so its ceiling is reporting depth and the 5,000 API calls per day. Pipedrive and monday CRM have no free tier at all — the paid step is day one, which is a filter in your favor if you want a tool that never dangles a free tier to convert you. If the follow-up habit is why you want a CRM, start on the free tier that covers your current headcount and budget the paid step at the next hire — the free tier was never going to hold you past that. Our free CRM guide maps the free ladder in full, and our cheapest CRM roundup covers the budget math across vendors.

## The options, side by side

| CRM | Starting price | Free tier | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Freshsales | $9/user/mo (Growth, annual) | Yes, up to 3 users | Cheapest real sales tool, built-in comms |
| Bigin by Zoho | $7/user/mo (Express, annual) | Yes, 1 user | Micro-teams of one or two |
| monday CRM | $12/seat/mo (Basic, annual) | 14-day trial only | Visual workflows, operations-heavy teams |
| Zoho CRM | $14/user/mo (Standard, annual) | Yes, up to 3 users | Most room to grow |
| Pipedrive | $14/seat/mo (Lite, annual) | 14-day trial only | Pipeline-first selling |
| Less Annoying CRM | $15/user/mo flat | 30-day trial | Simplest possible decision |
| HubSpot | $0 → Starter $20/seat/mo (list) | Yes, 2 users | Starting at $0, marketing in one place |
| Salesforce Starter Suite | $25/user/mo | 30-day trial | Planning to scale into Salesforce |

Prices researched 2026-11-10 from vendor pricing pages and current third-party pricing reads (Pipedrive per its own pricing page, checked directly today; Zoho free tier per its own pricing page; HubSpot, monday CRM, Freshsales, Bigin, Less Annoying CRM, and Salesforce Starter Suite per at least two independent sources each, including vendor-checked roundups dated September–October 2026). All prices are per user or seat per month on annual billing unless noted, excluding taxes. Vendors reprice and re-tier regularly — confirm your exact tier before committing.

## What a 5-person team actually pays

The headline price is not the bill. Here is the monthly license cost for five seats, on annual billing:

| CRM | Plan for 5 seats | Monthly cost (5 seats) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bigin | Express $7/user | $35 |
| Freshsales | Growth $9/user | $45 |
| monday CRM | Basic $12/seat | $60 |
| Zoho CRM | Standard $14/user | $70 |
| Pipedrive | Lite $14/seat | $70 |
| Less Annoying CRM | Flat $15/user | $75 |
| HubSpot | Starter $20/seat (list) | $100 |
| Salesforce Starter Suite | $25/user | $125 |

Two things to notice. First, the spread from cheapest to most expensive is $90 a month — $1,080 a year — for tools whose core job is identical. Second, HubSpot’s free tier does not appear in this table at all: it covers 2 users, so a 5-person team cannot run on it for free, and its list-price Starter is the second most expensive option here. The promotional $7/seat Starter rate for new customers on annual billing would bring a 5-seat HubSpot bill to $35 a month — but it is a new-customer promotion, so budget from the $20 list price and treat the promo as a discount, not the price.

## The CRMs, product by product

### Freshsales — the cheapest real sales tool ($9/user/month)

Freshsales (Freshworks CRM) is the pick for a team that wants phone, email, and chat inside the CRM instead of bolted on. Growth starts at $9/user/month billed annually, and it includes a kanban pipeline view, contact lifecycle stages, and built-in chat, email, and phone — the communication tools other CRMs charge extra for or push to an integration. The free plan covers up to 3 users with contact and deal management, so a team of three can run it at $0 until the fourth hire.

Two honest cautions. First, the features that make a CRM feel smart — contact scoring, sequences, and territory management — start at Pro ($39/user/month), so Growth is a communication-first tier, not an automation-first one. Second, Freshsales is a sales workspace, not an all-in-one platform: if you later want marketing automation or service tickets in the same system, you are buying more Freshworks products, not extending this one. Best for: small teams that handle a high volume of calls and emails and want everything in one tool at the lowest paid price on this list.

### Bigin by Zoho — the micro-team pick ($7/user/month)

Bigin is Zoho’s lightweight CRM, built for teams that want a pipeline and nothing else. Express starts at $7/user/month billed annually ($9 month-to-month), and the free plan covers 1 user with a 15-day trial of the premium features. It is pipeline-centric by design: contacts, deals, and follow-ups in a simple workflow, with none of Zoho CRM’s configuration depth.

Two honest cautions. First, it is deliberately limited — no forecasting, no lead scoring, no complex sales operations — so a team that grows into those needs will migrate to Zoho CRM proper, which is a rebuild, not an upgrade. Second, at $7 a seat it is the cheapest paid option here, but only because it does the least; compare it against Zoho CRM’s free tier (3 users, $0) before paying for Bigin, because a three-person team may not need to pay anything at all yet. Best for: one- or two-person teams that want the cheapest possible paid CRM and a pipeline they can set up in an hour.

### monday CRM — the visual pick for operations-heavy teams ($12/seat/month)

monday CRM is the pick when the sales process is visual and the team also runs operations in the same place. Basic starts at $12/seat/month billed annually, with flexible boards, fields, automations, and cross-team workflows that other CRMs in this price band do not offer. There is no free tier — only a 14-day trial — and plans start from a 3-seat minimum, so the smallest possible bill is $36 a month.

Two honest cautions. First, the minimum-seat rule means a two-person team pays for a third seat it does not have; at that size, Bigin or HubSpot free is cheaper. Second, automation limits vary by tier, and the boards are so flexible that a team without discipline ends up with a system only one person understands — the same trap as a spreadsheet, with a subscription attached. Best for: teams of 3 to 10 that sell and deliver in the same system and think in boards, not lists.

### Zoho CRM — the most room to grow ($14/user/month)

Zoho CRM punches well above its price point: custom fields, workflows, and modules that rival enterprise CRMs at a fraction of the cost. Standard starts at $14/user/month billed annually, and the free plan covers up to 3 users with contact management, workflow automation, standard reports, and 5,000 API calls per day — the most generous free tier on this list by capability, not just headcount. The upgrade path runs through Professional ($23/user/month) to Enterprise, and the wider Zoho One ecosystem (books, mail, desk) is there if the business grows into it.

Two honest cautions. First, it needs more setup and administration than the lightweight CRMs here — budget an afternoon to configure it properly, and expect the person who sets it up to become the de facto admin. Second, Zoho’s pricing pages push you toward a quote calculator for the higher tiers, so get a real number for Professional or Enterprise before budgeting a move up. Best for: growing small teams that need enterprise-level customization without enterprise pricing, and that can spare an afternoon of setup.

### Pipedrive — the pipeline-first pick ($14/seat/month)

Pipedrive was built by salespeople, and it shows: the entire interface is organized around a visual pipeline where you drag deals between stages, and it strips away the complexity that bogs down other CRMs. Lite starts at $14/seat/month billed annually ($168 per seat per year), confirmed on its pricing page today, with lead, calendar, and pipeline management, 500+ integrations, and meeting intelligence. There is no free tier — a 14-day trial, no credit card required.

Two honest cautions. First, email sync and automations start above Lite, at Growth ($39/seat/month) — so the cheapest tier is genuinely a pipeline and a contact list, and the automation most teams eventually want costs nearly three times as much. Second, the per-seat price is identical to Zoho Standard, but Zoho gives you a free tier and far more configuration for the same money — Pipedrive earns its price on focus, not features. Best for: sales-driven small teams that want a CRM focused on pipeline management and deal velocity, and nothing else.

### Less Annoying CRM — the simplest possible decision ($15/user/month)

Less Annoying CRM does exactly what the name promises: one plan, one price, no tiers, no upsells. $15/user/month flat, with a 30-day trial. It is a straightforward contact and pipeline manager designed for small businesses that want no feature-gating and no pricing puzzle — the bill for a 5-person team is $75 a month, today and next year.

Two honest cautions. First, simplicity is the whole product: there is no marketing automation, no advanced reporting, and no ecosystem to grow into — a team that outgrows it migrates, full stop. Second, at $15 a seat it costs more than Freshsales Growth and Bigin Express while doing less than either, so you are paying a premium for the absence of decisions. That is a fair trade for a team that has been burned by upsell pricing, and a bad trade for a team that wants the most capability per dollar. Best for: very small teams (1–10 people) that want a CRM they can explain in one sentence and never think about again.

### HubSpot — the free start, and the most expensive habit ($0; Starter $20/seat)

HubSpot is the only free CRM here that feels like a real product rather than a trial: contact management, a deal pipeline, email tracking, and a meeting scheduler for $0, with no expiration — and the free tier holds up to 1,000,000 contacts. For a two-person team’s first year, that is genuinely enough: import your contacts, set up the pipeline, connect your inbox, and build the follow-up habit before spending anything.

The design is the funnel, and it is worth understanding: the caps are engineered to convert you exactly when you grow. The 2-user limit forces a paid seat at your third hire. Starter lists at $20 per seat per month (currently shown at a $7 promotional rate for new customers on annual billing). Real sales automation waits at Professional, $90 per seat per month plus a mandatory one-time $1,500 onboarding fee — at 5 seats, that is $450 a month plus $1,500, against Freshsales Growth at $45. And HubSpot was built for sales and marketing teams that want both in one ecosystem: if that is your shape, the premium buys something real; if you only need a pipeline, it does not. Best for: teams that want a free starting point with room to grow into marketing automation in the same system — and that understand the paid tiers escalate fast.

### Salesforce Starter Suite — the scale-later mention ($25/user/month)

Salesforce Starter Suite is the entry point into the Salesforce ecosystem: $25/user/month on monthly or annual billing, with a 30-day trial and a free Suite that supports up to 2 users. It is the most expensive option on this list per seat, and the only one whose real value is what it leads to — the full Salesforce platform, AppExchange, and enterprise customization.

The honest read: a small team buys Starter Suite for the future, not the present. More advanced customization, automation, and AppExchange access sit in Pro, and the platform’s complexity is the price of its depth. Unless your team has a specific reason to end up on Salesforce — a parent company, an industry integration, a hiring plan that points that way — the $25 a seat buys less small-team usability than the $9 Freshsales tier. Best for: teams planning to scale fast into a Salesforce-shaped future, and almost nobody else at this size.

## The four traps that decide the real bill

1. The headline price is not the bill — headcount is. A $14/seat tool is $70 a month for five people and $140 for ten. Before comparing features, multiply every price by your headcount, then by 12. The $90-a-month spread between Bigin and Salesforce Starter at five seats is $1,080 a year — enough to matter, and invisible in a feature comparison that never mentions seats.

2. The minimum seat count. monday CRM plans start from 3 seats, so a two-person team pays $36 a month for a seat nobody sits in. HubSpot free covers 2 users and no more. Check the minimum and the free-tier cap together: the cheapest tool for a two-person team is not the cheapest tool for a five-person team.

3. The automation cliff. Pipedrive Lite at $14 has no email sync or automations — those start at Growth, $39. HubSpot free has no real automation — that starts at Professional, $90 plus $1,500 onboarding. The tier that does the job you actually want is often two or three times the starting price, and the starting price is the one in the headline. Price the tier you will need in six months, not the tier you can start on today.

4. The CRM nobody opens. This is the trap that costs the most and appears on no pricing page. A CRM’s value is the follow-up it produces, and follow-up only happens if the team updates it. The tool that wins is the one the least technical person on the team will open every morning. If you are choosing between two tools and one of them needs an admin, you do not have an admin — pick the other one. Our CRM cost guide maps the full ladder across vendors, our honest CRM test settles whether a CRM earns its keep at your size, and CRM vs. spreadsheet settles the comparison in detail.

## The verdict: best for each small-team shape

Cheapest real sales tool: Freshsales Growth ($9/user/month billed annually). Pipeline, email, phone, and chat in one place; free up to 3 users.

Most room to grow: Zoho CRM Standard ($14/user/month billed annually). Free for up to 3 users, enterprise-level customization, upgrade path to Professional and beyond.

Pipeline-first selling: Pipedrive Lite ($14/seat/month billed annually). The whole interface is the pipeline; email sync and automation wait at Growth ($39).

Visual workflows and operations: monday CRM Basic ($12/seat/month billed annually). Boards, fields, and cross-team workflows — with a 3-seat minimum.

Micro-team of one or two: Bigin Express ($7/user/month billed annually). The cheapest paid CRM here; check Zoho CRM’s free tier first, since it covers 3 users at $0.

Two people, zero budget: HubSpot free. Real pipeline, real email tracking, $0 — and a clear-eyed view of the Starter and Professional prices waiting above it.

Simplest possible decision: Less Annoying CRM ($15/user/month flat). One plan, one price, no tiers — the premium buys the absence of decisions.

Planning to scale into Salesforce: Salesforce Starter Suite ($25/user/month). The most expensive per seat here, and only worth it if the future is Salesforce-shaped.

Still deciding how a CRM fits your team, or what one should cost a business your size? Our simple CRM guide covers the easiest options in more depth, our free CRM guide maps the free ladder, our CRM cost guide maps the full price ladder, and the CRM category hub maps every comparison we’ve published — including HubSpot vs. Pipedrive and Pipedrive vs. Zoho CRM if your shortlist has narrowed to two.

Prices checked 2026-11-10 from vendor pricing pages and current third-party pricing reads (Pipedrive per its own pricing page, checked directly today; Zoho free tier per its own pricing page; HubSpot, monday CRM, Freshsales, Bigin, Less Annoying CRM, and Salesforce Starter Suite per at least two independent sources each, including vendor-checked roundups dated September–October 2026). Capsule’s free tier (2 users, 250 contacts) is consistent across sources; its Professional price is $18/user/month billed annually per the majority of current 2026 reads, though a minority of aggregators still show older $12 figures — confirm on the vendor’s pricing page. Vendors reprice and re-tier regularly — confirm your exact tier on the vendor’s pricing page before committing.

## Frequently asked questions

What is the best CRM for a small team?

It depends on how your team sells and how many seats you need. Freshsales Growth at $9/user/month billed annually is the cheapest paid pick with real sales tools and built-in phone, email, and chat. Zoho CRM Standard at $14/user/month billed annually is the pick for the most room to grow, with a free tier for up to 3 users. Pipedrive Lite at $14/seat/month billed annually is the pick for a team that lives in its pipeline. monday CRM Basic at $12/seat/month billed annually is the pick for visual, operations-heavy teams. Bigin Express at $7/user/month billed annually is the pick for micro-teams of one or two. HubSpot free at $0 is where a team of two should start.

How much does a CRM cost for a 5-person team?

At annual billing, a 5-person team pays about $35 a month for Bigin Express ($7/user), $45 for Freshsales Growth ($9/user), $60 for monday CRM Basic ($12/seat), $70 for Zoho CRM Standard or Pipedrive Lite ($14 each), $75 for Less Annoying CRM ($15/user flat), $100 for HubSpot Starter at list price ($20/seat), and $125 for Salesforce Starter Suite ($25/user). HubSpot's free tier covers only 2 users, so a 5-person team cannot run on it for free. Those are license costs only — none of these charge implementation fees at this size, which is part of why they suit small teams.

Is there a free CRM for small teams?

Yes, and the free tiers are genuinely usable at this size — but each one ends at a different headcount. HubSpot free covers 2 users and 1,000 marketing contacts with no expiration. Zoho CRM free covers up to 3 users. Freshsales free covers up to 3 users. Bigin free covers 1 user. Capsule free covers 2 users and 250 contacts. Pipedrive and monday CRM have no free tier, only a 14-day trial. The seat cap is the real limit: the day your fourth colleague needs a login, HubSpot free is done and Zoho free is done too.

What is the difference between a CRM for a small team and an enterprise CRM?

A small-team CRM is designed to be set up in an afternoon by the person who will also use it — no administrator, no consultant, no implementation project. An enterprise CRM like Salesforce or Microsoft Dynamics assumes a dedicated admin, custom objects, approval chains, and territory management, and prices accordingly. The practical difference is who does the work: with a small-team CRM the owner configures it; with an enterprise CRM you hire someone to configure it. A team of 2 to 10 people almost never needs the enterprise half of the feature list, and pays for it anyway if it buys the enterprise tool.

Do small teams need a CRM, or is a spreadsheet enough?

A spreadsheet works until two things happen: more than one person needs to update the same customer record, and follow-ups start slipping because nobody owns the next step. A CRM earns its keep when it answers three questions a spreadsheet cannot answer reliably — who did we last talk to, what did we promise, and when do we follow up — without anyone remembering to maintain it. Our honest CRM test walks through the decision, and CRM vs. spreadsheet settles the comparison in detail.

Which CRM is easiest for a non-technical small team?

Less Annoying CRM and Bigin are the simplest by design: one plan, minimal settings, and a pipeline you can explain in a minute. Pipedrive is the simplest of the full-featured options — its whole interface is the pipeline. HubSpot free is easy to start but gets complicated fast once you leave the free tier, because its pricing is built around upselling you into Professional features. Zoho CRM is the most powerful for the money and the most fiddly to set up; budget an afternoon, not an hour.

Keep every customer conversation connected. Integrate your preferred email service with Zoho CRM. Send, receive, and track emails—all in one place. Create automated workflows that nurture leads, send follow-ups, set reminders for callbacks, and keep conversations moving forward. Trigger the right action at the right time based on customer responses.

## Frequently Asked Questions

When should I upgrade to the Standard Edition?

If your team is spending time on manual processes, needs more customization, or requires advanced sales management features such as workflows, reporting, and multiple pipelines, Zoho CRM's Standard Edition can help you work more efficiently and grow.

Can I upgrade from the Free edition at any time?

Yes, you can upgrade from the Free Edition to the Standard Edition at any time. Your existing data, records, and configurations remain intact, allowing your team to continue working without disruption while gaining access to additional features and capabilities.

Who is the Standard Edition best suited for?

The Standard Edition is ideal for small and growing businesses that have outgrown basic Zoho CRM requirements and need more automation, customization, reporting, and sales management capabilities to grow further.

How is the Standard Edition better than the Free Edition?

The Free Edition helps businesses get started with the basics of Zoho CRM and the Standard Edition unlocks advanced features and capabilities like workflows, assignment rules, cadences, multiple pipelines, built-in calling, unlimited reports, and integrations with Marketplace, to name just a few. This helps teams save time, improve productivity, and manage sales more effectively.

What other key features come with Standard Edition?

The Standard Edition also includes features like Canvas, which lets you customize the Zoho CRM interface without coding, and Kiosk, which helps streamline data entry and record updates through guided experiences. These features make it easier to tailor Zoho CRM to your business needs and improve user adoption.
